raw_case_text:
A 9-month-old boy, 2nd progeny of a nonconsanguineous marriage presented with generalized skin rash and fever for 1 week. Three days before the onset of symptoms, he had running nose and loose stools which settled spontaneously over the next 2 days. Routine blood investigations done before presentation revealed anemia (haemoglobin 6.8 g/dl) with borderline normal total leukocyte count (4000/cu mm). Other blood counts were not available. He received antibiotics (intravenous injection ceftriaxone and injection amikacin and also oral amoxicillin) and packed red blood cells (approximately 40 ml/kg of body weight). The indication for blood transfusion was not clear, and child was transfused with group matched whole blood (one unit) donated by his uncle. High-grade fever and rash developed 3 days following the packed cell transfusion. The rash was initially noticed on the trunk which spread over face and limbs, eyes, and involved mucosa of oral cavity. There was no history of abortions or sibling deaths in the family.
Examination revealed a sick looking child, with generalized plethoric skin with papules and vesicles filled with clear fluid along with peeling of the skin involving entire body and oral mucosa. Conjunctival membrane was involved with eyelid edema and mucopurulent discharge. He was febrile and irritable but hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination was remarkable for hepatosplenomegaly while examination of other systems was within normal limits. Investigations of the child at presentation to our center are summarized in Table 1.
He was started on broad spectrum antibiotics. Work up done for infectious etiology including blood culture, urine culture, malarial antigen test, serology for dengue, chikungunya, leptospirosis, and rickettsia was negative. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polymerase chain reaction in urine was positive with 12000 copies/ml which may explain the pretransfusion anemia and low normal total counts. However, possibility of transfusion associated CMV transmission cannot be ruled out. Screening for autoimmunity (Direct Coomb's test and antinuclear antibody) was noncontributory. Incidentally, serum vitamin B 12 was found to be 91 pg/mL (normal range 200-835 pg/mL), probably contributing to pancytopenia. General condition of the child deteriorated further by day 3 of hospitalization, with persistent fever and bleeding per rectum. Blood counts further decreased on day 3 with total leukocyte count 700/cu mm, and platelet count of 25,000/cu mm; however, haemoglobin remained at 16.2 g%. S. Ferritin was 2529 ng/ml. In view of fever, pancytopenia, organomegaly, raised serum ferritin a possibility of hemophagocytic syndrome was considered, and a bone marrow aspirate was performed but it was inconclusive.
On day 4, C-reactive protein was increased to 185 mg/L. However, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was only 5 mm/h, probably reflecting hypofibrinogenemia in the present clinical context. He was treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and steroids as per hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) protocol. Total counts decreased to 370/cu mm at day 5 with worsening of liver functions. He succumbed to death on day 8 of hospitalization due to refractory shock. Postmortem bone marrow biopsy [Figure 1a] showed extensive hemophagocytosis; skin biopsy [Figure 1b] showed acanthosis; and presence of necrotic keratinocytes in the epidermis suggestive of toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and liver biopsy revealed micro and macro steatosis. Multiple triggers, namely, CMV infection, massive blood transfusion, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), all of which may predispose to hemophagocytic syndrome were identified in the patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-month-old boy presented with a 1-week history of high-grade fever and generalized vesiculobullous and desquamating skin rash involving the body, eyes, and oral mucosa.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to presentation, the infant had a 2-day self-limiting episode of rhinorrhea and loose stools. Subsequent outside blood work showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL) and borderline leukocyte count (4,000/cu mm), for which he received IV ceftriaxone, IV amikacin, oral amoxicillin, and a transfusion of 1 unit (~40 mL/kg) of group-matched whole blood/packed RBCs donated by his uncle. Three days post-transfusion, he developed high-grade fever and a generalized rash starting on the trunk and spreading to the face, limbs, conjunctivae, and oral mucosa over 1 week. By day 3 of hospitalization at the referral center, he deteriorated with persistent fever and rectal bleeding.
subjective.past_medical_history: Second child of a nonconsanguineous marriage. Recent antibiotic exposure (ceftriaxone, amikacin, amoxicillin) and related-donor blood transfusion from his uncle 10 days prior. No family history of spontaneous abortions or sibling deaths.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, generalized blistering/peeling skin rash, oral mucosal lesions, ocular discharge/eyelid swelling, irritability, and subsequent hematochezia; preceding coryza and loose stools resolved.

objective.physical_examination: Sick-looking, febrile, irritable, and hemodynamically stable infant on admission. Dermatological and mucosal exam showed generalized plethoric skin with fluid-filled papules and vesicles and extensive epidermal peeling across the entire body, oral mucosal involvement, conjunctival involvement, eyelid edema, and mucopurulent ocular discharge. Abdominal exam revealed hepatosplenomegaly; other systemic examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-referral blood counts: hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 4,000/cu mm. Referral hospital labs: serum vitamin B12 91 pg/mL (reference 200-835 pg/mL). Infectious workup: blood culture, urine culture, malarial antigen test, and serologies for dengue, chikungunya, leptospirosis, and rickettsia all negative. Direct Coombs test: negative. Day 3 labs: total leukocyte count dropped to 700/cu mm, platelets 25,000/cu mm, hemoglobin 16.2 g/dL, serum ferritin 2,529 ng/mL. Day 4 labs: C-reactive protein (CRP) 185 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 5 mm/h (attributed to hypofibrinogenemia). Day 5 labs: total leukocyte count 370/cu mm with worsening liver function tests.
objective.advanced_workup: Urine CMV PCR: positive at 12,000 copies/mL. Antinuclear antibody (ANA): negative. Antemortem bone marrow aspirate (day 3): inconclusive. Postmortem biopsies: bone marrow biopsy demonstrated extensive hemophagocytosis; skin biopsy showed acanthosis and epidermal necrotic keratinocytes consistent with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN); liver biopsy showed microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) / Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) overlap, triggered by cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, drug exposure, and/or transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (following uncle-donated blood transfusion), with underlying vitamin B12 deficiency. Malaria, dengue, chikungunya, leptospirosis, rickettsial infection, and bacterial sepsis were excluded. Confirmation: Urine CMV PCR positive (12,000 copies/mL), hyperferritinemia (2,529 ng/mL), severe pancytopenia, and postmortem bone marrow, skin, and liver biopsies confirming extensive hemophagocytosis, TEN, and hepatic steatosis. Management and outcome: Treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), and corticosteroids per HLH protocol; despite treatment, the infant developed progressive leukopenia (370/cu mm), hepatic dysfunction, and died on hospital day 8 from refractory shock.
